name: lightsout
description: The built-in TypeScript standards: rules that keep a repo the same shape at every level, correct what models get wrong by default and settle code style, 36 of them with a deterministic check.

packs.name: code-style
packs.description: Makes code read the same whoever wrote it: one way to write a function, a class, a named value and a unit test.

packs.name: fractal
packs.description: Keeps the repo the same shape at every level, so any file's place is predictable and a duplicate is found by searching for its name.

packs.name: react
packs.description: The rules written for React: size caps for hooks and components, and one way to write a component test.

packs.name: standards
packs.description: For a package with no framework pack of its own: one shape at every level, written in one style.

packs.name: tanstack-start
packs.description: The rules written for TanStack Start: which of its files get unit tests.

topics.intro:
# Classes

When to write a class, and how classes share behaviour.

# Functions

How a function takes its arguments, returns, and declares its values.

# Named Constants

A set of named string values, written as a `const` object with a union type derived from it. A named constant is that object. A value constant is any other constant.

# Type Safety

Proving a value's type instead of switching the check off.

# Duplication

How code is kept free of copies and dead code, and named so that a search finds it.

A method that only passes a call on to a collaborator its class holds is never a copy, however many classes hold the same collaborator.

# Imports

How an import names the file it reads from, and what a package makes public.

- An index file is `index.ts`, or the same name in any other dialect: `index.js`, `index.mjs`, `index.jsx`, `index.tsx`.
- A package's entry is the index file its manifest publishes to other packages. It sits at the package root or its `src/`, or the manifest names it, as a subpath export such as `"./contracts": "./src/contracts/index.ts"` does. It is the package's public contract: it lists exactly what other packages may use.

# Layout

Every folder under `src/` is one of three kinds.

**A module** is one export and the code only it uses. It is one file, named after its export. It becomes a folder, with a main file of the same name, only when it needs files of its own, and goes back to a file when the folder is down to one. The folder takes its export's name and casing, so a class folder is PascalCase: `HttpClient/HttpClient.ts`. Everything in the folder except the main file is private to the module.

**A subject folder** groups modules about one subject, such as `billing/` or `git/`, and has no main file. Everything at its top level is public. The top folders of `src/` are subject folders.

**`common/`** holds what a folder's contents share. It sits in the lowest folder that contains every file using it, and is private to that folder. Functions and classes sit directly in it, types in `common/types/`, constants in `common/constants/`. A file with both a type and a value goes by its value.

Never make any other kind of folder.

# Size

How long a function, a file and a folder may grow before it is split.

# React

How React code is written: components, hooks and JSX.

# Test Style

How unit tests are arranged, asserted and mocked.

- A setup factory is a function named `setup…` that arranges one test and returns what the test needs.

# Test Placement

Where unit tests sit, what they cover and how large they grow.

- A module is one export and the code only it uses: a file, or a folder whose main file is named after it.
- A public file is a top-level file of a subject folder, or a module folder's main file. A file in a `common/`, and every other file in a module folder, is private.
- An index file is `index.ts`, or the same name in another dialect such as `index.tsx`. A package's entry is the index file its manifest publishes to other packages.

# Unit Testing Components & Hooks

How React and Preact components and hooks are unit-tested.

# Testing a TanStack Start App

Which files of a TanStack Start application get unit tests.

rules.name: lightsout/assertions-pin-contracts
rules.summary: What a test asserts against.
rules.prose:
## Assertions Pin Contracts

- Assert against literals. Never import a constant from the module under test into its own assertions: comparing a value to itself passes even when the value is wrong. The literal is the contract's independent second statement, not duplication. Constants from other modules, such as shared enums, are fine as inputs.
- Pin machine-facing values exactly: error codes, event names, API fields. Pin human-facing text, such as UI copy and log messages, loosely, with `stringContaining` or a regex, or not at all, so a wording change fails no contract test.
- Assert what the unit does: its output, or a side effect at its boundary, such as an injected repository called with the right arguments. Never assert that an input comes back unchanged, unless exposing it is the unit's job: for a class whose job is to resolve and expose state, its public fields are its output. Never reach into what a consumer never touches, such as private helpers or caches.

rules.name: lightsout/banned-folder-name
rules.summary: Folder names that say nothing about what the folder holds.
rules.prose:
## Banned Folder Name

Name a folder for its subject, such as `billing/` or `formatting/`, never for the kind of code it holds.

- `utils/`, `services/`, `helpers/`, `lib/`, `core/`, `misc/`, `shared/` and `internal/` are never folder names.
- `types/` and `constants/` are folder names only at the top of a `common/`.

A name that says nothing about what a folder holds draws code nobody placed, and `common/` is the only folder name with a meaning of its own.

fixtures.text: export const getInvoice = () => 1;
export const formatAmount = () => 1;

rules.name: lightsout/case-collision
rules.summary: Names that differ only in upper and lower case.
rules.prose:
## Case Collision

Never put two siblings in a folder whose names differ only by case, including a file beside a folder: `readme.md` beside `README.md`, or `Gates.ts` beside `gates/`. Rename one of them.

A case-insensitive filesystem such as macOS or Windows sees one entry where Linux CI sees two, so an import can reach a different file on the machine that checks it, and a type checker objects late or, in plain JavaScript, never.

fixtures.text: export { renderGreeting } from './gates/renderGreeting';
export const renderGreeting = (): string => 'hello';
declare module '*.md';
export { renderGreeting } from './gates/renderGreeting';
export const renderGreeting = (): string => 'hello';
export const Markdown = () => <section>markdown</section>;

rules.name: lightsout/circular-dependencies
rules.summary: Modules that depend on each other.
rules.prose:
## Circular Dependencies

Never let two modules import each other. Move the piece they share, usually a type, into a third module both import, or move code as `file-placement` says.

A cycle makes load order fragile and breaks tree-shaking.

fixtures.text: export type CustomerTier = 'gold' | 'standard';

import type { CustomerTier } from '../common/types/CustomerTier';

export const getCustomerTier = ({ lifetimeCents }: { lifetimeCents: number }): CustomerTier => (lifetimeCents > 100_000 ? 'gold' : 'standard');

rules.name: lightsout/class-inheritance
rules.summary: Sharing behaviour between classes.
rules.prose:
## Class Inheritance

Never share behaviour through `extends`. Share by composition: hold the common part as a value the composer creates and passes in, and delegate to it. State contracts as interfaces; `implements` is not inheritance.

- `Error` is the one base you may extend, including an error family such as `extends HttpError`, because subclassing is the only way to make a typed error that `instanceof` can check.
- When a framework's contract is a base class, extending it is allowed. Treat a decorated class as framework-owned.

A base class couples every subclass to its internals: a change or an override acts at a distance, and what is shared hides in a second file.

rules.name: lightsout/common-folder-layout
rules.summary: What the inside of a common folder looks like.
rules.prose:
## Common Folder Layout

Inside `common/`:

- A function or class sits directly in `common/`.
- A type goes in `common/types/`, a constant in `common/constants/`. A value not written as a function or class is a constant, one built by a call included.
- Make no other folder until `common/` holds more than 20 files. Then group its functions into subject folders, such as `formatting/`.

Then where a shared file goes is never a choice, and a reader knows where to look.

fixtures.text:
// Correct: a constant, so it goes in common/constants/.
export const rateLimits = { min: 0, max: 1 } as const;

rules.name: lightsout/component-test-rendering
rules.summary: Where a component test renders and queries.

rules.name: lightsout/constant-casing
rules.summary: How a constant's name is cased.
rules.prose:
## Constant Casing

Name a `const` object that shares its name with its type in PascalCase, such as `Action`. Name every other constant in camelCase: a single value such as `maxRetries`, or an object that groups related values such as `featureThresholds`.

rules.name: lightsout/dead-export
rules.summary: Code that nothing uses any more.
rules.prose:
## Dead Export

Delete an export that nothing references, not even a test, as soon as it becomes unused. This covers interfaces, types and functions as well as values.

- Never keep code in case it is needed later: version history still has it.
- When you are not sure whether something is used, search before you delete it.

Unused code still has to be read, and kept compiling, by everyone who passes it.

fixtures.text: export const buildGreeting = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => `Hello, ${name}.`;

import { buildGreeting } from './buildGreeting'; export const renderGreeting = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => `

${buildGreeting({ name })}

`;

export const renderGreeting = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => `

Hello, ${name}.

`;

rules.name: lightsout/duplicate-code-block
rules.summary: The same code written out in more than one place.
rules.prose:
## Duplicate Code Block

When the same code appears in two or more files, such as loading and error handling, validation or a repeated transformation, write it once where `file-placement` says, and import it.

Copies drift apart, and a fix then reaches only one of them.

rules.name: lightsout/duplicate-export-name
rules.summary: Exports in different places that share one name.
rules.prose:
## Duplicate Export Name

Within a package, give every export a name no other export has. Before you add an export, search the package for that name.

- The same thing written twice: keep one, and move it where `file-placement` says.
- Two different things: rename one, so each name says what it is.

Then a search by name finds the one place a concept lives.

fixtures.text: export const formatAmount = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
export const formatAmount = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

rules.name: lightsout/duplicate-function-body
rules.summary: Functions that are copies of each other under new names.
rules.prose:
## Duplicate Function Body

Never write a function whose body is another function's with only the names or the literal values changed. Keep one, and pass the values that differed as arguments.

- This covers every function, method and callback, in the same file or another.

Renaming a copy hides it from a search by name, so the two drift apart unseen.

rules.name: lightsout/existing-tests
rules.summary: How these rules apply to a repo's existing tests.
rules.prose:
## Existing Tests

These rules describe the tests you write, not a mandate to rewrite the ones already there. When a repo's tests use an older style, such as `beforeEach` with a shared `let`, or nested `describe` blocks:

- When you extend an existing test file, match its style, and never mix a second style into it. A blocking rule still holds in every test you add or change.
- When you create a test file, follow these rules, even when the test you mirror uses the older style. Mirror its coverage, not its structure.
- Never rewrite passing older tests to these rules during a feature task. That is cleanup with its own review.

Following this order is normal work, with nothing to report. Report it only when this rule failed you, because the conflict was not about style, or it was unclear which case applied.

fixtures.text: export const getLabel = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => name.trim();
export const getLabel = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => name.trim();

rules.name: lightsout/explicit-return-type
rules.summary: When a function's return type is written out.
rules.prose:
## Explicit Return Type

Declare the return type of every exported function. Leave it to inference everywhere else.

- An exported function needs none when its type is already written elsewhere: a generic signature, a method implementing an interface, or a variable typed with a function type.
- Keep an annotation on an internal function only when removing it changes what the compiler accepts, such as a recursive helper.
- An existing exported function gains its return type when you next edit it.

The return type is the output half of an export's contract. Written out, a change to it shows in the diff and fails where it is defined, not in a caller.

rules.name: lightsout/file-placement
rules.summary: Where a file belongs, from who uses it.
rules.prose:
## File Placement

Put a file where its users are.

- Used by one file: beside that file, in its module folder.
- Used by two or more files: in the `common/` of the lowest folder that holds them all.
- Used from outside its subject folder: at the top level of that subject folder.

When a file gains a user, move it, update the imports, and check the move made no circular imports.

Then where a file sits shows who uses it.

fixtures.text:
// Correct: both files of the chargeCustomer module use this, and no file outside it.
export const roundCents = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): number => Math.round(cents);

import { taxRate } from './taxRate.ts';

export const refundCustomer = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): number => cents * taxRate;

rules.name: lightsout/file-size
rules.summary: How long a file may grow.
rules.prose:
## File Size

Keep a file to 250 lines or fewer. At the cap, split the file, or turn its module into a folder as `module-file-to-folder` says.

An index file is exempt: a package's entry is its public API, and it cannot take the remedy a size finding asks for.

rules.name: lightsout/filename-mismatch
rules.summary: How a file's name follows what it exports.
rules.prose:
## Filename Mismatch

Name a file exactly as its export, casing included: `buildVersionedLabel.ts`, `UserProfile.ts`. A file with a union and its member types takes the union's name.

A file named like its export is found by searching for the export.

fixtures.text: export const getChargeLabel = ({ amount }: { amount: number }): string => `${amount}`;
export const getChargeLabel = ({ amount }: { amount: number }): string => `${amount}`;
export const getChargeTotal = ({ amount }: { amount: number }): number => amount;

rules.name: lightsout/folder-size
rules.summary: When a folder holds too many files.
rules.prose:
## Folder Size

When a folder holds more than 20 files, not counting tests, group related files into subject folders named for what they share.

- A module folder counts as one file.
- `types/` and `constants/` are exempt: they hold files only.

A long flat folder reads like a listing instead of a description of the product.

rules.name: lightsout/function-size
rules.summary: How long a function may grow.
rules.prose:
## Function Size

Split a function longer than 80 lines. Lines run from the signature to the closing brace, and a callback with no name counts toward the function that holds it.

Extract a piece because it deserves a name, not to win back lines.

rules.name: lightsout/import-path-alias
rules.summary: When imports use the package's path aliases.
rules.prose:
## Import Path Alias

Use the package's configured path alias for every import. A package has aliases when it declares `imports` in `package.json` or `compilerOptions.paths` in `tsconfig.json`, and then never uses a relative path (`./`, `../`), not even for a sibling file, a `common/` subfolder or a package entry's re-exports.

When a package declares no aliases, use relative paths consistently.

Read the alias from the package's own declaration; never write one from memory, because packages differ.

A `paths` alias, declared in `tsconfig.json`. It takes no file extension:

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
"paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] }
```

```typescript
import { features } from '@/features/home/common/constants/features';
```

An `imports` alias, declared in `package.json`. It names the real file, so it carries the extension:

```jsonc
// package.json
"imports": { "#src/*": "./src/*" }
```

```typescript
import { features } from '#src/features/home/common/constants/features.ts';
```

Incorrect in a package with either alias:

```typescript
import { features } from './common/constants/features';
```

Then every import of a file reads the same, wherever it is written.

fixtures.text:
import { formatRate } from '@/common/utils/formatRate';

export const getChargeLabel = (): string => formatRate();
export const formatRate = (): string => '1';

import { formatRate } from '../common/utils/formatRate';

export const getChargeLabel = (): string => formatRate();
export const formatRate = (): string => '1';

rules.name: lightsout/index-file-contents
rules.summary: What an index file may hold.
rules.prose:
## Index File Contents

An index file holds only re-export lines, `export { Foo } from '<path>'` and `export type { Bar } from '<path>'`, and comments.

- Re-export each name explicitly, never with `export *`. List what other packages need, and nothing only the package itself uses.
- Put executable code in an entry file with its own name, conventionally `main.ts`, which imports what it runs from the files that declare it.

A package's entry is the list other packages build against. Code in it makes that list hard to read, and a star publishes whatever its target happens to export, so the contract stops being a decision.

fixtures.text: export const renderGreeting = (): string => 'hello';
export { renderGreeting } from './feature/renderGreeting';

import { renderGreeting } from './feature/renderGreeting';

console.log(renderGreeting());
export const renderGreeting = (): string => 'hello';

rules.name: lightsout/index-files
rules.summary: Which folders have an index file, and where an import points.
rules.prose:
## Index Files

Only a package's entry is an index file, and nothing inside the package imports through it. Every import names the file that declares what it imports: `@/ingestion/ingestRecords`, never `@/ingestion`.

- Delete an index file in any other folder, and import each name from the file that declares it.
- Import from another package through its entry, such as `@acme/engine`, never by a path into its `src/`.
- An index file may re-export from another index file, and its own test imports it.

An import through an index file loads every file it re-exports to reach one name, and a test runner, unlike a bundler, pays for all of them.

fixtures.text: export { ingestRecords } from './ingestion/ingestRecords';
export const normalizeRecord = (): number => 1;

import { normalizeRecord } from './common/utils/normalizeRecord';

export const ingestRecords = (): number => normalizeRecord();

import { ingestRecords } from '../ingestion/ingestRecords';

export const buildReport = (): number => ingestRecords();
export const normalizeRecord = (): number => 1;
export { ingestRecords } from './ingestRecords';

import { normalizeRecord } from './common/utils/normalizeRecord';

export const ingestRecords = (): number => normalizeRecord();

import { ingestRecords } from '../ingestion';

export const buildReport = (): number => ingestRecords();

rules.name: lightsout/module-boundary-testing
rules.summary: Testing a module through what it makes public.
rules.prose:
## Module Boundary Testing

Test a module through its public file, and cover the files only it uses through that file.

- A public file is a top-level file of a subject folder, or a module folder's main file. Each gets a test beside it.
- A file in `common/` gets a test of its own: several callers rely on it.
- A file private to one module gets a test of its own only when its cases are too many to drive through the public file, when it is a contract that stands alone, such as a parser, or when coverage a gate demands cannot be reached through the public file.
- A file with no logic, such as a type, a constant of fixed values or an index file, gets no test.
- An existing direct test stays. When a new test could go either way, write it against the public file.

A branch no input reaches, through the public file or directly, is dead code: delete it instead of testing it.

A test through the public file pins behaviour, not how the module is split inside, so the insides can be reorganised without touching a test.

fixtures.text: export const normalizeRecord = ({ raw }: { raw: string }): string => raw.trim();

import { normalizeRecord } from './common/utils/normalizeRecord';

export const ingestRecords = ({ raw }: { raw: string[] }): string[] => raw.map((record) => normalizeRecord({ raw: record }));
export const normalizeRecord = ({ raw }: { raw: string }): string => raw.trim();

import { normalizeRecord } from './common/utils/normalizeRecord';

export const ingestRecords = ({ raw }: { raw: string[] }): string[] => raw.map((record) => normalizeRecord({ raw: record }));

rules.name: lightsout/module-file-to-folder
rules.summary: When a module should stay one file, and when it should become a folder.
rules.prose:
## Module File to Folder

Keep a module in one file until it needs files of its own. When a module folder holds only its main file, turn it back into a file.

fixtures.text: export const getDelay = ({ attempt }: { attempt: number }): number => 100 * 2 ** attempt;

rules.name: lightsout/multi-export
rules.summary: How many things one file may export.

fixtures.text:
import type { Config } from '@/common/types/Config';

export const defaultConfig: Config = { name: 'default' };

export const SyncState = { idle: 'idle', busy: 'busy' } as const;

export type SyncState = (typeof SyncState)[keyof typeof SyncState];

rules.name: lightsout/named-string-values
rules.summary: How a set of named string values is declared and used.

rules.name: lightsout/no-any
rules.summary: Avoiding the type that switches type checking off.
rules.prose:
## No Any

Never use `any`. When a type is genuinely unknown, use `unknown` and narrow it with type guards. When it is not, write the specific type or a generic. A rare, justified exception gets the project's lint-suppression comment, with the reason.

`any` switches type checking off for everything it touches.

fixtures.text: export const parseRecord = ({ raw }: { raw: unknown }): string => String(raw);
export const parseRecord = ({ raw }: { raw: any }): string => String(raw);

rules.name: lightsout/no-route-file-tests
rules.summary: Whether a route file gets a unit test.
rules.prose:
## No Route File Tests

Never write a unit test for a route file under `routes/`. Test the screen the route renders instead.

A route file is thin wiring: guards, layout and one screen render. The screen's own tests and the end-to-end tests cover it.

fixtures.text:
// The screen the `/issues` route renders. export const IssuesScreen = () =>

Issues

;

rules.name: lightsout/no-test-state-in-hooks
rules.summary: Where a test's state is built.
rules.prose:
## No Test State in Hooks

Never build a test's state in a `beforeEach`. Build it in the setup factory, which each test calls:

- Never keep test state, the subject under test included, in a `let` that a `beforeEach` reassigns. Return it from the setup factory as a `const`.
- Set a mock's return value or implementation (`mockReturnValue`, `mockResolvedValue`, `mockRejectedValue`, `mockImplementation`) in the setup factory, never in a `beforeEach`.
- Act and assert in the `test`, never in a `beforeEach`.

Then each test states its own arrangement, and none depends on what another left behind.

rules.name: lightsout/object-args
rules.summary: How a function takes its arguments.
rules.prose:
## Object Args

Give a function that takes arguments one object argument, and destructure it:

- An exported function declares an interface named `Params` for it.
- A private helper uses an inline object type, since one file cannot declare two `Params`.
- A function with no arguments takes no object and has no `Params`.

Two signatures follow a contract set elsewhere, and are never declared again locally: a callback, whose caller sets its shape, and a wrapper that passes its params object on unchanged, typed `Parameters<typeof callee>[0]`.

When callers need to name the argument type, export it as a named type in place of `Params`.

Positional arguments decay as a function grows: new ones are added out of order, and two of one type swap silently (`copyFile(dest, src)` compiles). A named argument says what it is at every call.

rules.name: lightsout/prefer-arrow-functions
rules.summary: Which form a function is written in.
rules.prose:
## Prefer Arrow Functions

Write functions as arrow functions.

Then every function in a codebase is declared the same way.

rules.name: lightsout/prefer-functions
rules.summary: When to write a class instead of functions.
rules.prose:
## Prefer Functions

Default to functions. Write a class if, and only if, at least one of these holds:

- **(a)** Mutable state persists across method calls: a `RateLimiter` counting its remaining tokens, a cache, a connection pool.
- **(b)** Three or more operations share injected config or dependencies: an `HttpClient` whose base URL, retries and credentials are injected once and used by every method.
- **(c)** Several implementations share one interface: `FileSource` and `S3Source` behind a `RecordSource` contract.
- **(d)** A framework requires it, because its dependency injection needs classes.

When none holds, write functions in a module. To check, ask whether "how many of these exist right now?" is a meaningful question: two `HttpClient`s pointed at different APIs, yes, so a class; two `formatDate`s, no, so a function.

Two shapes never pass that test:

- A class with only static members. It is a module in disguise: it adds a `ClassName.` prefix to every call and binds no state. Write module functions instead.
- A stateless class with one method, such as `class ReportGenerator { execute() }`. Write the function.

A class that is decorated, is abstract, or implements or extends another type is not one of these shapes; the four criteria above judge it.

Keep a class's methods to behaviour that needs its state. Put other logic in functions rather than instance methods: logic that needs no state is easier to read and reuse as a function.

rules.name: lightsout/react-function-size
rules.summary: How long a function, a hook and a component may grow.
rules.prose:
## React Function Size

Split a function longer than 80 lines. A hook, a function whose name starts with `use`, may run to 160 lines, and a component, a capitalised function in a `.tsx` file, may run to 200. Lines run from the signature to the closing brace, and a callback with no name counts toward the function that holds it.

Extract a piece because it deserves a name, not to win back lines.

rules.name: lightsout/reuse-common-code
rules.summary: Look for existing shared code before writing new code.
rules.prose:
## Reuse Common Code

Before you write a helper, type or constant, look for one in every `common/` folder in the package.

- If one does what you need, import it. Never write a second copy.
- If it sits in another module's `common/`, move it up as `file-placement` says, then import it.
- If one nearly does, extend it rather than write a near copy, as long as its current callers keep working.

Two copies drift apart, and a fix then reaches only one of them.

fixtures.text:
// Shared by getChargeLabel and getInvoiceLabel, so it lives in src/common/utils/.
export const formatMoney = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

import { formatMoney } from './common/utils/formatMoney.ts';

export const getChargeLabel = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `Charged ${formatMoney({ cents })}`;

// Shared by getChargeLabel and getInvoiceLabel, so it lives in src/common/utils/.
export const formatMoney = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

import { formatMoney } from './common/utils/formatMoney.ts';

export const getChargeLabel = ({ cents }: { cents: number }): string => `Charged ${formatMoney({ cents })}`;

rules.name: lightsout/shared-package-criteria
rules.summary: What belongs in the shared package.
rules.prose:
## Shared Package Criteria

In a repo with several packages, never copy code from one package into another. Put it in the shared package, but only when two or more packages need it and it is a contract both sides agree on, such as constants, error codes or pure functions.

- One package needs it: put it in that package's `common/`.
- It depends on a library only one package uses: keep the pure part shared, and wrap it in that package.

Copies in each package drift apart, and a fix then reaches only one of them.

fixtures.text: export const getInvoiceRowClass = () => 'row';
export const hasPermission = () => true;

import { getInvoiceRowClass } from '@scope/shared/billing/utils/getInvoiceRowClass';

export const renderInvoiceRow = getInvoiceRowClass;
export const getInvoiceRowClass = () => 'row';

rules.name: lightsout/single-return
rules.summary: Where a function returns its result.

rules.name: lightsout/single-use-scalar
rules.summary: Where a value used in only one place is declared.
rules.prose:
## Single-Use Scalar

Declare a scalar that is read in only one place where it is read, not at module scope: `const maxRetries = 10;` inside the function, not `const MAX_RETRIES = 10;` at the top of the module. Hoist it to module scope only when two or more places read it, or when it is a lookup map or structured config.

A value declared beside its only reader is read without a jump to find it.

rules.name: lightsout/test-beside-subject
rules.summary: Where a unit test file sits, and what it is named.
rules.prose:
## Test Beside Subject

Put a unit test beside the one source file it tests, and name it after that file: `src/auth/AuthService.ts` is tested by `src/auth/AuthService.unit.test.ts`. The part of the test's name before the first dot names a real file in the same folder.

- Never put a unit test in a `__tests__/`, `tests/` or `test/` folder under `src/`.
- A test that covers several source files is split into one test file per source file.
- When one subject genuinely needs more than one test file, such as a pipeline with distinct scenarios, add a camelCase scenario to the name: `<File>.<scenario>.unit.test.ts`, such as `runImplementPipeline.monorepo.unit.test.ts`.

Then a file's test is found beside it, under its name.

fixtures.text: export const getLabel = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => name.trim();
export const getLabel = ({ name }: { name: string }): string => name.trim();

rules.name: lightsout/test-code-path-coverage
rules.summary: Which tests a unit needs.
rules.prose:
## Test Code Path Coverage

Cover every code path: branches, error handling and boundary conditions. Give each path one test, and never add a test that only varies the input. Inputs that take one path to different outputs share one `test.each`.

To reach a branch that guards against input the types forbid, such as a `default` arm or an early return on an impossible discriminant, force the input with `as unknown as T`. That and the stub cast `test-mock-untyped` allows are the only casts a test writes.

rules.name: lightsout/test-file-size
rules.summary: When a test file is too long.
rules.prose:
## Test File Size

Keep a test file to 400 lines or fewer. Past the cap, split it by named scenario, one concern per file: `runPipeline.supervisor.unit.test.ts`, `runPipeline.advisories.unit.test.ts`.

Never split a test file into unnamed halves, or delete assertions, to get under the cap.

rules.name: lightsout/test-jest-imports
rules.summary: What a test file imports from Jest.
rules.prose:
## Test Jest Imports

Import the test functions by name from `@jest/globals`, as the file's first import: `import { describe, expect, test } from '@jest/globals';`. Add `jest` only when the file uses `jest.fn`, `jest.mock` or `jest.spyOn`, and `beforeEach`, `afterEach` or `afterAll` only when the file needs one.

rules.name: lightsout/test-manual-mock-cleanup
rules.summary: Resetting mocks between tests.
rules.prose:
## Test Manual Mock Cleanup

Leave mock cleanup to the package's Jest config, `clearMocks: true` and `restoreMocks: true`. Never clean mocks by hand in a `beforeEach`, `beforeAll`, `afterEach` or `afterAll`: no `jest.clearAllMocks()`, `jest.resetAllMocks()`, `jest.restoreAllMocks()`, `mockClear()` or `mockReset()` there.

When the package's config lacks them, never add them. That changes every existing test in the package, so it is the repo owner's decision, not a test task's side effect. Instead:

- Build fresh `jest.fn()` mocks, and a fresh subject, inside each setup factory call.
- Reset a module-level mock that must persist, such as one a `jest.mock` factory reads, at the top of the setup factory with `.mockReset()`, and wire it again. Or assert on it only with `toHaveBeenCalledWith`, which earlier calls cannot fool, and never with `not.toHaveBeenCalled`.
- Report the missing config.

rules.name: lightsout/test-mock-prefix
rules.summary: How mocks are named.
rules.prose:
## Test Mock Prefix

Start the name of every mock declared at module scope with `mock`, such as `mockGetProfile`. Jest hoists `jest.mock()` calls to the top of the file, and only `mock`-prefixed variables are reachable inside the factory.

rules.name: lightsout/test-mock-untyped
rules.summary: Typing a mock function and the wrapper that forwards to it.

rules.name: lightsout/test-structure

rules.name: lightsout/test-support-in-src
rules.summary: Where shared test helpers, mocks and fixtures live.
rules.prose:
## Test Support in Src

Keep shared test helpers, mocks and fixtures out of `src/`, in the package's `tests/` folder: `tests/helpers/`, `tests/mocks/`, `tests/fixtures/`. Only test files sit beside their source.

- A mock or helper one test file uses stays in that file.
- One that several test files share goes in `tests/`.

Under `src/`, test-support code reads as production source, to scanners and people alike.

rules.name: lightsout/what-to-mock
rules.summary: What to mock, and with which tool.
rules.prose:
## What to Mock

Construct the subject under test directly, and stub only the boundaries you do not own: the network, the filesystem, other modules' services. Never mock what you own and could simply build.

- Use `jest.spyOn` for one method on an object you already hold, such as an injected service or repository; the rest stays real.
- Use `jest.mock` for a standalone function exported from another module.
- Never mock a module that only exports plain constants; import the real one, since mocking it blocks coverage and adds no isolation. Mock one only when it has import-time side effects, or when the test needs a different value, and then prefer `jest.replaceProperty` or injection.
